title: 2026-03-12 Redwood deep dive: Private VPC networking & runtime performance
summary: Deep technical session focused on Private VPC deployment patterns for Redwood Private. Covered networking options (PrivateLink vs ENI/peering), egress/NAT constraints for model pulls and metrics, DNS and private hosted zones, and runtime impacts (KV cache, batching, quantization). Identified next steps: share architecture diagram, security docs, schedule benchmark run in Lexicon VPC, propose pilot config and pricing.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Ava Brooks (Redwood AE), Samuel Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Lexicon Lead Infra), Martin Reyes (Network), Leah Kim (Security), Tom Alvarez (ML Eng)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): discussion about PrivateLink and VPC networking, NAT egress for model artifacts, DNS resolution for private endpoints, and runtime tuning for latency/throughput.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:00] Ava (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for carving out the time. we wanted to run a deep dive on the private vpc architecture and how that ties into runtime perf, batching, kv cache, all that. how's that timeline look for you?
[00:00:12] Priya (Lexicon): yes thanks, ava. we have a few folks on from infra and security. primary ask: we need a private deployment with no internet egress for customer data, minimal attack surface, and predictable latency for our triage system.
[00:00:25] Samuel (Redwood SE): cool, that's exactly what Redwood Private with a VPC control plane can support. quick clarifier: when you say no internet egress, do you mean outbound to S3 for model pulls is disallowed or just not allowed for runtime model downloads?
[00:00:34] Martin (Network): ideally both; we have strict egress rules. images and model artifacts must be pulled through our internal artifact repo, and anything external has to go through a controlled NAT with logging.
[00:00:00] Ava (Redwood): noted. we often see two patterns: 1) full PrivateLink control plane where all control plane APIs are interface endpoints in your account and we never go over public internet, or 2) a hybrid where you allow outbound to specific S3 prefixes via VPC endpoints or a dedicated NAT with strict route tables. both have tradeoffs.
[00:01:10] Tom (ML Eng): can you explain the PrivateLink path? we heard it's more expensive, but lower attack surface?
[00:01:22] Samuel (Redwood SE): yeah. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) puts an ENI in your subnet and traffic goes over AWS backbone to Redwood's control plane. pros: private, no public IPs, supports TLS and mTLS. cons: per-hour and per-GB pricing on aws side and the ENI counts if you need high throughput. also need to size subnets to handle ENI scale.
[00:01:45] Leah (Security): does PrivateLink avoid NAT entirely for control plane calls?
[00:01:50] Samuel (Redwood SE): yes for control plane. runtime inference traffic can be kept wholly in your VPC if you run the private runtime in the same account—no NAT for model serving traffic. but for artifacts pulled from external registries you either need S3 gateway endpoints or an outbound NAT with proxy.
[00:02:12] Martin (Network): okay, sizing: for our predicted baseline of 200 rps with bursts to 1200, what ENI and subnet counts would we expect?
[00:02:20] Samuel (Redwood SE): rough rule: each interface endpoint scales to some concurrent flows but we recommend multiple AZ subnets and at least a /24 per AZ to avoid running out of IPs once you allocate worker ENIs, lb ENIs, and PrivateLink ENIs. for 200–1200 rps you'll want autoscaling across several nodes, and to ensure route table limits and ENI quotas are increased. we can provide a worksheet with numbers.
[00:02:48] Ava (Redwood): also important: long-lived connections for streaming (server-sent events / websocket-ish streaming) benefit from TCP keep-alive and HTTP/2 with connection reuse. that reduces handshake overhead which matters for latency SLOs under 100ms.
[00:03:05] Priya (Lexicon): we measure p50 around 70ms internally for simple requests; need p95 below 250ms. how does KV cache and batching impact that?
[00:03:15] Samuel (Redwood SE): KV cache (our kv cache is for key/value attention cache reuse across requests) cuts generation latency for repeated prefixes by avoiding recomputation. but cache locality matters: if your requests hit different workers or you have ephemeral workers without shared cache, you'll see misses. for private deployments we recommend colocating the cache and workers—either shared in-process or via a memcached/redis within the VPC. note: sometimes transcribers write KV as "KV cash" in our notes so ignore that mis-typo.
[00:03:49] Tom (ML Eng): are there networking implications for cache when using a remote redis—tcp latency adds to token latency, right?
[00:03:55] Samuel (Redwood SE): yes. roundtrip to a redis can add 0.5–3ms depending on placement—if the model needs per-token fetches, that can add up. we have an option to colocate an in-memory shared cache per host which avoids network hops at the cost of memory. that's often recommended for low-latency workloads.
[00:04:20] Martin (Network): about DNS — we use private hosted zones and split-horizon. how do we ensure service discovery for Redwood endpoints?
[00:04:27] Samuel (Redwood SE): we support private hosted zone entries and recommend creating interface endpoints with the AWS-assigned DNS names; you can also create alias records in your zone pointing to the endpoint. if you have custom DNS forwarders, ensure they resolve the private endpoint names to the VPC-internal ENI IPs and not public addresses.
[00:04:45] Leah (Security): what about audit logs and flow logs? we'd need VPC flow logs, ELB access logs, and audit of API calls.
[00:04:53] Ava (Redwood): Redwood Private ships with audit logging hooks and can push to your SIEM via CloudWatch logs or a customer-managed S3 bucket. for network flows we recommend enabling VPC flow logs and sending them to the same logging pipeline. we'll share our audit schema in the security pack.
[00:05:08] Priya (Lexicon): you mentioned control plane — do we need outbound internet to contact your control plane if we use PrivateLink?
[00:05:15] Samuel (Redwood SE): with PrivateLink, no. the only thing that might require outbound is pulling images from public registries or pulling prebuilt quantized kernels if you opt in for Redwood-managed binaries. alternatively, you can host binaries/artifacts in your internal repo and configure our deployer to fetch from there.
[00:05:30] Tom (ML Eng): for quantization and deployment, any special networking for model shards or optimized kernels?
[00:05:36] Samuel (Redwood SE): model files are typically stored in S3-like stores; we support presigned URLs over PrivateLink or direct S3 gateway endpoints. quantized kernels are local artifacts once deployed. for large model loads we recommend using staged deployments per-AZ so that initial load traffic doesn't saturate a single NAT/router.
[00:05:56] Martin (Network): staging, good point—so we should do per-AZ pre-warm pulls. how much bandwidth do you expect for a 7B model?
[00:06:04] Samuel (Redwood SE): roughly 3–6GB for a 7B depending on quantization; might be larger if you use fp16 or non-quantized. plan for tens of G to allow parallel pulls; stagger pulls or use local caching to limit burst issues.
[00:06:18] Priya (Lexicon): on encryption and KMS — if we want envelope encryption with our KMS, can Redwood integrate?
[00:06:24] Ava (Redwood): yes, we support customer-managed KMS for at-rest artifacts and can integrate with HSM for keys in private deployments. we'll include the integration guide.
[00:06:33] Leah (Security): SSO and SAML for console? RBAC?
[00:06:37] Ava (Redwood): yes, SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning supported for the control plane console; for private control plane we mirror roles and can integrate with your IdP.
[00:06:46] Tom (ML Eng): back to runtime perf—how does batching interact with latency? our traffic is chatty and we can't afford big batch delays.
[00:06:54] Samuel (Redwood SE): batching is a tradeoff: batching increases throughput and reduces per-token cost, but adds queuing latency. Redwood Optimize provides adaptive batching: it will batch opportunistically up to a latency SLO you set. for chatty workloads we recommend a small max batch size with an aggressive timeout (e.g., 20ms) to keep p95 reasonable. also connection reuse and HTTP/2 multiplexing reduce the per-request overhead so tiny batches are less costly.
[00:07:20] Tom (ML Eng): do we have observability hooks to measure kv cache hit rates, batch sizes, and per-token latency?
[00:07:25] Ava (Redwood): yes, the console exposes token-level latency, batch size histograms, and cache hit rates; we can also add tracing headers to correlate requests end-to-end.
[00:07:36] Martin (Network): let's talk about egress — our compliance requires all outbound to go through a proxy with logging. can Redwood send telemetry via that proxy?
[00:07:44] Samuel (Redwood SE): yes, you can configure our runtime to route outbound through a customer-managed HTTP proxy or NAT. some control plane telemetry can be proxied via PrivateLink too. we can also disable outbound telemetry if you require full air-gap; in that case we provide an offline bundle and on-prem install instructions.
[00:08:03] Priya (Lexicon): offline install is attractive. is that a different licensing tier?
[00:08:07] Ava (Redwood): generally yes, private air-gapped installs are part of our enterprise/private licensing and involve some professional services to bootstrap.
[00:08:15] Leah (Security): about connecting to our on-prem data — do you recommend Direct Connect or a VPN?
[00:08:20] Samuel (Redwood SE): Direct Connect + private virtual interface is lower latency and more stable, but more setup. VPN works fine for pilot and smaller throughput. choose based on bandwidth and SLA needs.
[00:08:31] Tom (ML Eng): any recommendations for load balancers in front of the runtime?
[00:08:35] Samuel (Redwood SE): we recommend either NLB for TCP-level with TLS passthrough or ALB for HTTP-level with TLS termination. NLB with TLS on the backend keeps handshake overhead low for streaming. ensure idle timeouts and keep-alive are tuned for long-lived streams.
[00:08:52] Priya (Lexicon): does the runtime open many outbound connections to control plane or is it single long-lived connection?
[00:08:58] Samuel (Redwood SE): control plane uses short request/response for management, and we establish long-lived multiplexed connections for streaming when needed. the number of concurrent connections depends on worker count; again sizing worksheet will help.
[00:09:12] Martin (Network): about route tables and NAT — do you recommend single NAT per AZ or a centralized NAT?
[00:09:18] Samuel (Redwood SE): AZ-local NATs minimize cross-AZ traffic and reduce latency. central NATs can be simpler but may create a single egress bottleneck. for high-throughput workloads, per-AZ NATs behind an autoscaling fleet is better.
[00:09:32] Ava (Redwood): a couple of real-world gotchas we've seen: 1) people forget DNS caching TTLs and end up with old ENIs; set short TTLs during rollout. 2) subnet IP exhaustion when autoscaling worker pools. 3) S3 endpoint policies blocking presigned URLs — need to test artifact access from the runtime subnets.
[00:09:52] Tom (ML Eng): do you recommend any specific kernel/quantization knobs to limit memory and network pressure?
[00:09:59] Samuel (Redwood SE): for 7B we usually recommend 4-bit quant (Q4) which cuts footprint and speeds up deserializa—sorry deserialization and memory. Q8 is also an option for accuracy. reduced memory reduces page faults which reduces network retransmits during scale events.
[00:10:15] Priya (Lexicon): are there any compliance artifacts you can share? SOC2, penetration test reports, architecture diagrams?
[00:10:21] Ava (Redwood): yes we'll share SOC2 type II summary, pen test redacted report, and a recommended VPC architecture diagram.
[00:10:29] Martin (Network): operationally, if we hit capacity constraints, do you support graceful degradation to a smaller model or fallback routing?
[00:10:36] Ava (Redwood): yes Redwood runtime supports model variants and automatic fallback routing by policy—route to a cheaper quantized variant in a different capacity pool. this keeps the service online albeit with potential quality differences.
[00:10:48] Leah (Security): one more on logging — can logs be pushed only to our S3 bucket and never retained by Redwood?
[00:10:54] Samuel (Redwood SE): yes, in private deployments you control log destinations. we can disable retention on Redwood side and write to your bucket with lifecycle rules.
[00:11:03] Tom (ML Eng): ok let's talk briefly about a benchmark run — can we run a perf test inside our VPC with your team present?
[00:11:10] Ava (Redwood): absolutely. typical approach: we provide a deployment artifact and a test harness; we run throughput and latency tests with your NAT/proxy and measure batch sizes, cache hits, p95 token latency. we'll need an account, subnets, and a test S3 or internal repo with model artifacts.
[00:11:27] Priya (Lexicon): timeline — we're aiming for pilot in 6 weeks. compliance sign-off might take 3–4 weeks.
[00:11:34] Ava (Redwood): that sounds reasonable. high-level next steps we'll capture.

[00:11:45] (crosstalk) Martin: kl —
[00:11:48] Ava: quick recap...
[00:11:50] Ava (Redwood): recap: 1) we'll send recommended VPC diagram and IP/subnet worksheet; 2) security docs (SOC2, pen test) and KMS integration guide; 3) propose pilot config including per-AZ NAT recommendations and PrivateLink option; 4) schedule benchmark run with Redwood SEs in your VPC; 5) provide price estimate for private deployment and air-gapped install if needed.
[00:12:14] Priya (Lexicon): yes please include cost tradeoffs for PrivateLink vs NAT and an estimate for egress bandwidth costs.
[00:12:20] Ava (Redwood): will do.
[00:12:24] Tom (ML Eng): one more question — for per-token tracing, is there PII risk in traces?
[00:12:29] Leah (Security): yeah we have to ensure traces are scrubbed.
[00:12:31] Ava (Redwood): we have redaction controls and can disable traces or scrub at ingest; we'll include tracing data handling in the security docs.
[00:12:39] Martin (Network): ok thanks everyone.
[00:12:43] Ava (Redwood): thanks all. we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[00:12:49] (meeting ends)
